blocks.text: What it does

holds a finite resource inventory, split into qualified and held contents. A tank, pantry, fuel stock, nutrient bin or waste receiver can all be represented by a Store. It does not process, purify or move material.
Ports
Inventory in accepts outputs from Transfers and processes; Inventory out supplies their inputs. Both allow multiple connections. The connected machine determines the required unit and composition.

rows.name: Unit
rows.description: One of g, kg, mL, L, m3, mol, kJ, MJ, Wh, kWh. All inventory/capacity numbers use this unit.

rows.name: Capacity
rows.description: Positive upper bound on qualified plus held contents.

rows.name: Starting usable / startingQualified
rows.description: Qualified contents at initialization.

rows.name: Starting held / startingUnqualified
rows.description: Contents awaiting processing; together with usable stock must fit capacity.

rows.name: Protected reserve
rows.description: Amount of qualified stock withheld from discretionary use; cannot exceed starting qualified inventory.

rows.name: Material identity
rows.description: Optional lowercase hyphenated material ID for observations/grouping; empty means unclassified.

rows.name: Declared composition
rows.description: Enables compound accounting; requires g or kg. Moisture, dry fractions and chemical energy describe the starting/declared material.

blocks.text: Example

a kg drinking-water Store holds 500 kg, starts with 300 kg usable and protects 100 kg. Crew consumes water; a surplus Transfer may refill a separate Electrolyzer feed tank without spending the protected portion. Use a compound declaration for the Crew water Store, as its port requires one.
What it does
moves qualified material between two Stores without changing its material composition, either continuously or as scheduled batches.
Ports

Source joins one Store's Inventory out; Destination joins a different Store's Inventory in. Transfer unit must exactly match both Stores (g to kg is not automatic). Compound endpoints normally need matching declared compositions; compound-to-plain movement is refused. The supported plain-water dilution exception permits plain inflow into a compound treatment water port, adding water only rather than inventing the destination's dry load.

rows.name: Mode
rows.description: Continuous rate or Scheduled inventory event.

rows.name: Unit
rows.description: Shared native unit of source, destination and transfer.

rows.name: Rate per second
rows.description: Positive continuous request in native units/s; inventory, reserve and headroom may limit it.

rows.name: Quantity
rows.description: Positive Scheduled request per occurrence.

rows.name: First occurrence / recurrence
rows.description: Scheduled timing; recurrence zero is one-off.

rows.name: Priority
rows.description: Orders competing transfers/events.

blocks.text: Continuous physical connections obey throughput and efficiency. Scheduled transfers are instantaneous, lossless, non-physical events: they respect inventory/reservations/headroom, but not physical cable/pipe ratings. A partial batch completes that occurrence; it is not retried or carried into the next.
Example

a recurring Scheduled Transfer moves food from a bulk Store to a small pantry every six hours. Crew consumes the pantry between restocks. If it empties early, Crew reports unmet food until a later restock.
What it does
transforms compound inputs into compound outputs at declared full-throughput rates. Use it for a material-processing recipe not already represented by a dedicated machine.
Ports

one to five Conversion input Stores and one to five Conversion output Stores. Every Store must be compound and mass-denominated; a Store may appear only once across the recipe. Different mass units are handled through mass accounting. Outputs may not create tracked constituents or chemical energy; deficits are explicitly accounted losses. Different compositions are allowed precisely because this is a conversion, not a Transfer.

rows.name: Input rate per second
rows.description: Positive native wet-mass units/s consumed at full operation for each input.

rows.name: Output yield per second
rows.description: Positive native wet-mass units/s produced for each output at that same full operation.

rows.name: Input/output count
rows.description: Growable sets, maximum five on each side.

rows.name: Priority
rows.description: Allocates competing conversion requests.

blocks.text: The limiting input or output headroom scales the whole recipe. There is no automatic electricity input or thermal output: do not assume this generic component models the energetics of an arbitrary real chemical reactor.
Example

separate a compound harvest Store into food and fibrous waste Stores, with each recipe's constituent and chemical-energy outputs funded by the input. This models a conservative sorting/processing boundary rather than turning a waste label into food for free.

An authored distribution circuit, placed from the Power group. Its input and output faces accept unlimited landings/taps. The inspector authors display name, rated capacity (0 is visibly Unrated) and trip persistence. Source/battery memberships and consumer Single/Transfer/Shared supply modes are authored in inspectors or by wiring. Rename/delete cascades all references and supports undo/redo. See Power Bus authoring. The older per-component descriptions of *automatic* electrical membership below refer to the legacy default-main topology, not an uneditable shared Power node; that derived node is retired. Transfer executes whole-load failover with a dwell-gated return (#882). Shared combines each bus's live post-protected spare pro-rata, preserving explicit unmet demand and applying the minimum-operable gate to the combined grant (#883). Breaker protection remains a separate follow-up (#884).

Each source or battery landing has its own cable throughput, efficiency and isolation state (#906). Multiple landings share one finite native source output or battery energy/rate budget; they do not copy capacity. Actual transfers are metered on the cable to the serving bus, including battery charging and refunded protected-service credits. Unused solar is availability rather than transmitted power; unused fuelled output is settled through the remaining live feeder budgets.
What it does
offers electricity according to installed capacity and a sunlight/eclipse profile.
Ports
automatic Power out to the shared electrical pool; no material input or manually wired power destination.

rows.name: Capacity kW
rows.description: Full-sun installed electrical capacity; zero disables the array.

rows.name: Illumination profile
rows.description: Fraction of full sun over simulation time; zero represents eclipse.

blocks.text: Example

an orbital Solar array supplies Equipment and charges a Battery in sunlight. During eclipse, the Battery and any dispatched Generator/Fuel cell must cover demand. Available solar capacity is not a guarantee of useful transmitted power through a constrained generation connection.
What it does

represents an external equipment load group: a laboratory, workshop, communications rack or other load not already modelled internally. Power, heat and any declared material exchanges scale together with admitted operation. Do not duplicate a Chiller's or Electrolyzer's own demand here.
Ports

automatic Power in. Up to two total material exchanges across Equipment input 1/2 and Equipment return 1/2, each naming a distinct Store; rates use that Store's native units. Material ports are optional, but once declared they constrain operation. Optional Heat out joins a Reservoir of the same thermal class only for Exported disposition. CoolingService instead uses the derived cooling service of its class; it cannot also name a passive heat sink.

rows.name: Electrical demand kW
rows.description: Full-operation electrical requirement.

rows.name: Operating profile
rows.description: Duty fraction applied over time.

rows.name: Heat output kW
rows.description: Full-operation heat output; scales with actual operation.

rows.name: Thermal class
rows.description: Required class of cooling service or declared heat sink.

rows.name: Cooling disposition
rows.description: Exported: explicit external heat boundary, or route to a Reservoir if named. CoolingService: requires available chilled service of its class.

rows.name: Critical floor kW
rows.description: Protected slice of this load's service, not an independent mini-load.

rows.name: Maximum curtailment
rows.description: Largest removable fraction of demand. 0 requires full operation; 1 permits complete curtailment. Below the minimum operable level the load is refused whole.

rows.name: Priority
rows.description: Ranks discretionary service allocation.

rows.name: Material rate / consumes
rows.description: Native units/s at full operation; consumes draws qualified surplus, return requires destination headroom.

rows.name: Recovery dwell seconds
rows.description: Minimum shed duration before a discretionary load may restart.

rows.name: Recovery hysteresis fraction
rows.description: Extra spare-power headroom above demand required for restart.

rows.name: Restart surge kW / seconds
rows.description: Extra startup demand and its duration. Recovery controls apply to purely discretionary loads, not loads with a critical floor.

blocks.text: Example

a workshop takes stock from one Store, returns waste to another, requests 5 kW and emits 4 kW into a matching Reservoir with a Radiator. A full waste Store throttles workshop operation, power and stock consumption together. It does not continue consuming electricity while silently deleting waste.
What it does
stores electrical energy, charges from surplus generation and discharges into deficits within power and reserve limits.
Ports
automatic Power in for charge and Power out for discharge; no authored material or heat-sink connector.

rows.name: Nameplate kWh
rows.description: Total installed energy capacity.

rows.name: Usable kWh
rows.description: Cyclable portion; reserve floor is nameplate − usable. Zero usable capacity disables the bank.

rows.name: Starting stored kWh
rows.description: Initial total stored energy, within nameplate. Energy below the reserve floor is not dischargeable.

rows.name: Maximum charge/discharge kW
rows.description: Separate limits on how quickly energy can enter or serve the bus.

rows.name: Charge/discharge efficiency
rows.description: Stored energy per input bus energy, and delivered bus energy per stored energy drawn; each in (0,1]. Losses are accounted.

blocks.text: Example

a 20 kWh usable bank supplying a 5 kW eclipse load lasts at most four hours before conversion/cable losses. A 2 kW discharge limit cannot supply that load in full even when the bank contains plenty of energy.
What it does
converts finite stored fuel energy into dispatchable electricity, with real startup draw, ramping, waste heat and shutdown heat. It is an energy contract, not a nuclear-reactor physics model.
Ports

Fuel in requires an energy Store (kJ, MJ, Wh or kWh). Heat out requires a same-class Reservoir. Automatic Power in funds startup and Power out supplies generation. Supervision accepts Outage and Maintenance references.

rows.name: Rated output kW
rows.description: Installed electrical ceiling; zero disables.

rows.name: Commanded output kW
rows.description: Manual dispatch request, between zero and rated. Automatic dispatch may replace the operating command.

rows.name: Efficiency
rows.description: Electrical output / consumed fuel energy, (0,1]; the remainder becomes waste heat.

rows.name: Maximum ramp kW/s
rows.description: Positive output slew limit, not an instantaneous step.

rows.name: Startup power kW / seconds
rows.description: Cranking draw and time that must actually be powered before running.

rows.name: Shutdown heat kW / seconds
rows.description: Continued heat after generation stops.

rows.name: Thermal class / heat sink
rows.description: Waste, startup and shutdown heat destination.

rows.name: Maximum sink temperature °C
rows.description: Cooling gate; the sink must be below it for qualified operation.

blocks.text: Example

a backup Generator draws from a finite kWh fuel Store and rejects heat to a Reservoir/Radiator plant. A Battery supplies cranking energy and bridges the ramp. Stopping the Generator does not remove its shutdown-cooling requirement, so protect the relevant Coolant loop/Chiller if needed.
What it does
consumes hydrogen and oxygen to generate electricity and product water; waste heat goes to its declared sink.
Ports

Hydrogen in, Oxygen in and Water out use plain mass Stores; reactants must not alias one inventory. Heat out requires a same-class Reservoir. Electricity automatically joins Power out. Use dedicated reactant Stores if breathing oxygen must remain separate: no hidden draw from an Atmosphere or life-support reserve exists.

rows.name: Chemistry
rows.description: PEM (default), alkaline or solid oxide. Persisted and shown in telemetry; currently descriptive only, with identical runtime behaviour and no chemistry-specific efficiency bands.

rows.name: Rated output kW
rows.description: Installed electrical rating; zero disables.

rows.name: Commanded output kW
rows.description: Dispatch request within rating; automatic dispatch can command backup output.

rows.name: Efficiency
rows.description: Electricity / hydrogen chemical energy, (0,1].

rows.name: Thermal class / sink
rows.description: Waste-heat interface.

rows.name: Maximum sink temperature °C
rows.description: Stops operation when cooling cannot accept the heat.

blocks.text: Example

Solar-powered Electrolyzers fill separate H2 and O2 Stores. A Fuel cell uses them during eclipse and sends water to a raw-water Store for Water treatment. Full water storage or exhausted reactants limits output; this cycle is storage with losses, not a self-powering loop.
What it does
performs CO2 + 4 H2 → CH4 + 2 H2O, recovering water from captured CO2 while retaining carbon in methane. Reaction heat and electrical process energy reach the heat sink.
Ports

CO2 in, Hydrogen in, Methane out, Water out each require a different plain mass Store. Heat out joins a same-class Reservoir; Power in is automatic. The process needs actual feed, electrical energy and product headroom together.

rows.name: Rate kg/s
rows.description: Rated CO2 feed conversion rate; zero disables.

rows.name: Specific energy kWh/kg CO2
rows.description: Electrical processing dose for actual conversion.

rows.name: Thermal class / sink
rows.description: Destination for reaction and process heat.

rows.name: Maximum sink temperature °C
rows.description: Cooling eligibility gate.

rows.name: Priority
rows.description: Processing power/service allocation order.

blocks.text: Example

CO2 capture fills a CO2 Store; an Electrolyzer supplies hydrogen. Sabatier returns water to the treatment chain and methane to a Methane processor. Account for heat rejection and net hydrogen demand rather than assuming all hydrogen recycles.
What it does
performs CH4 → C + 2 H2, producing solid carbon and recovering part of the hydrogen used by Sabatier. Electricity must fund the endothermic reaction; remaining process heat goes to its sink.
Ports
Methane in, Hydrogen out, Carbon out require distinct plain mass Stores. Heat out needs a same-class Reservoir; Power in is automatic.

rows.name: Rate kg/s
rows.description: Rated methane feed processing rate; zero disables.

rows.name: Specific energy kWh/kg CH4
rows.description: Must at least fund the reaction's heat demand; not an arbitrary free yield.

rows.name: Thermal class / sink
rows.description: Process-heat destination.

rows.name: Maximum sink temperature °C
rows.description: Cooling gate.

rows.name: Priority
rows.description: Processing allocation order.

blocks.text: Example

process Sabatier methane, return hydrogen to the shared H2 feed Store, and retain carbon in a finite Store with scheduled Waste ejection. A full carbon Store backpressures the chain. Recovered H2 is less than Sabatier consumed, so the combined loop still needs fresh hydrogen.
What it does

holds thermal energy in an effective thermal mass. Heat inputs change its temperature; hosted Radiators reject heat, loops exchange heat, and buffers temporarily absorb deficits. It is not an infinite heat sink.
Ports

Heat in accepts multiple compatible machine outputs and heat-only exchangers. Hosted radiators and Hosted buffers mount those components. Diagram direction does not make passive exchangers one-way; actual heat exchange can reverse with temperature. Heat-engine references can also use Reservoirs, but are not currently editable Flow ports.

rows.name: Thermal class
rows.description: Class of heat/service the reservoir supports.

rows.name: Heat capacity kJ/K
rows.description: Positive energy required for a one-degree temperature rise.

rows.name: Starting temperature °C
rows.description: Initial thermal state.

rows.name: Minimum/maximum temperature °C
rows.description: Service limits reported as crossings, not clamps or automatic thermostats.

rows.name: Absorbed heat kW
rows.description: Constant environmental heat input.

blocks.text: Example

a Generator emits heat into a generation Reservoir. A Radiator removes heat according to temperature and environment. Too little radiator area eventually heats the Reservoir above the Generator's cooling gate.
What it does

exchanges radiative heat with an external environment using emissivity × view factor × area × σ × (T⁴ − T_sink⁴) in absolute temperature. It is a real temperature-dependent rejection path, not a fixed cooling credit.
Ports
Host reservoir joins one Reservoir's Hosted radiators face. Multiple Radiators may share a host. There is no gas or coolant-mass input.

rows.name: Area m²
rows.description: Positive emitting area; more area increases exchange at the same temperatures.

rows.name: Emissivity
rows.description: Surface emission effectiveness, (0,1].

rows.name: View factor
rows.description: Effective view of the declared environment, (0,1].

rows.name: Sink temperature °C
rows.description: Effective radiative background, including back-radiation; not necessarily deep space.

blocks.text: Example

mount a panel on an equipment-heat Reservoir. Reduce its view factor to represent obscuration, or raise sink temperature for a warmer radiative environment. The resulting loss of rejection can exhaust a Thermal buffer and ultimately stop heat-producing equipment.
What it does

owns a finite, closed coolant inventory and pumps it through a heat-only exchanger with one Reservoir. It also models freeze-protection heating. Coolant never becomes drinking water or moves into another component.
Ports

Heat exchanger joins a Reservoir's Heat in. Cold interface serves a Chiller evaporator; at most one Chiller may claim a given loop. Cold surfaces serves Water collectors. Buffer gates can gate Thermal buffers. Power in is automatic; Supervision accepts Outage/Maintenance.

rows.name: Coolant capacity / starting coolant kg
rows.description: Maximum and initial internal inventory. Zero starting coolant disables circulation and heating.

rows.name: Specific heat kJ/kg·K
rows.description: Coolant thermal capacity per kg; combines with actual inventory to set temperature response.

rows.name: Starting temperature °C
rows.description: Initial coolant state.

rows.name: Pump power kW
rows.description: Electrical draw at full circulation.

rows.name: Rated flow kg/s
rows.description: Circulation rating; not a transfer of inventory out of the loop.

rows.name: Exchanger conductance kW/K
rows.description: Full-circulation heat coupling to the host Reservoir.

rows.name: Freeze-protection setpoint °C
rows.description: Thermostat threshold below which the heater requests power.

rows.name: Heater capacity kW
rows.description: Maximum freeze-protection electrical/heat input.

rows.name: Critical service
rows.description: Explicitly protects circulation/heating ahead of discretionary external loads.

blocks.text: Example

a loop exchanges heat with a cabin-cooling Reservoir and supplies a collector's cold surface. A Chiller extracts heat from that loop into a separate rejection Reservoir. During a pump Outage, collection and circulation-gated buffer access cease even if the loop still contains coolant.
What it does
spends electricity to extract heat from a circulating loop and rejects that heat plus electrical work/auxiliaries into a Reservoir. It also supplies the derived cooling service of its thermal class.
Ports

Cold loop joins one Coolant loop's Cold interface; Condenser heat joins a different Reservoir from the cold loop's host. The Chiller class must match both the cold host and condenser Reservoir. Power in is automatic; cooling-service output is derived. Supervision accepts Outage/Maintenance.

rows.name: Rated cooling capacity kW
rows.description: Maximum extracted heat, not electrical consumption; zero disables.

rows.name: COP
rows.description: Extracted heat per unit compressor work; work is cooling/COP. Positive authored assumption.

rows.name: Auxiliary power kW
rows.description: Additional running draw that also reaches the condenser.

rows.name: Chilled setpoint °C
rows.description: No extraction at/below this cold-loop temperature.

rows.name: Maximum condensing temperature °C
rows.description: No operation if the rejection sink is at/above it.

rows.name: Thermal class
rows.description: Required class of both interfaces and the cooling service supplied.

rows.name: Critical service
rows.description: Protects its deliverable electrical work before discretionary loads.

blocks.text: Example

a 3 kW cold duty at COP 3 requires 1 kW compressor work, plus any auxiliaries; the rejection plant must handle at least 4 kW. Pair the condenser Reservoir with a Radiator rather than assuming the Chiller deletes heat.
What it does
stores a finite amount of heat during its host Reservoir's cooling deficit and releases it when real rejection surplus returns. Its stored energy is separate from the host's thermal energy.
Ports
Host reservoir joins Hosted buffers. Circulation gate is required in circulation mode and must name a loop on that same Reservoir; passive mode needs no circulation gate.

rows.name: Access mode
rows.description: passive heat contact or circulation powered-loop access.

rows.name: Capacity kJ
rows.description: Total storable heat across the usable temperature band.

rows.name: Starting energy kJ
rows.description: Initial fill; determines remaining absorption headroom.

rows.name: Minimum/maximum usable temperature °C
rows.description: Band across which stored fraction maps to buffer temperature. A narrow band approximates phase-change storage.

rows.name: Maximum charge/discharge kW
rows.description: Separate rate limits for absorption/recovery.

rows.name: Transfer conductance kW/K
rows.description: Passive heat-transfer limit; positive in passive mode.

rows.name: Circulation loop
rows.description: Access prerequisite in circulation mode, not a coolant feed.

blocks.text: Heat must move down the temperature gradient. Empty storage alone does not permit absorption if the buffer is already hotter than its host.
Example

a passive thermal store absorbs an equipment plant's 2 kW deficit while a radiator is unavailable. A 7200 kJ empty buffer provides at most one hour at that deficit, subject to temperature and charge limits. Afterwards, recovering storage consumes actual spare radiator capacity; it is not instant.
What it does

conducts heat between two Thermal nodes without moving mass between Atmospheres, Reservoirs, and Electrolyzers with an authored Thermal body. Use it for a solid wall or shared structure, including reservoir meshes, without occupying a compartment's heat-only exchanger slot.
Ports

End A and End B each join an Atmosphere's or Reservoir's Thermal links face, or a bodied Electrolyzer's Thermal body face. Endpoints must resolve to distinct nodes with positive thermal capacity. Duplicate undirected pairs are refused; combine parallel contacts by summing conductances on one link. Thermal service class is ignored. Stores, bodyless machines and Exterior vacuum are not Thermal nodes. A body endpoint uses kind machineBody and the Electrolyzer ID. The apparent input faces are endpoint references, not a heat-flow direction.

rows.name: Conductance kW/K
rows.description: Positive overall heat coupling: instantaneous heat flow is G × (T_A − T_B). Includes area/material/thickness effects in one number.

rows.name: End A / End B
rows.description: Fix the sign of reported flux, not who may receive heat.

blocks.text: There is no separate area, openness, efficiency or throughput. Temperature difference drives passive exchange; the finite-capacity solve approaches thermal equilibrium rather than prescribing a constant heat rate.
Example

connect a warm laboratory and cool cabin with a Thermal link for their partition. Add a separate Atmosphere pathway for the doorway opening. Closing that pathway stops air-carried heat, but wall conduction continues. A link's conductance does not automatically follow door openness.

Endpoint kinds are reported in the link snapshot beside signed flow, cumulative net transfer and Idle/Active status. YAML and binary records retain the historical aAtmosphereId / bAtmosphereId names for node IDs and add aKind / bKind (atmosphere, reservoir or machineBody); omitted kinds default to atmosphere. Reservoirs publish conducted heat separately from exchanger heat, and both enter their energy residual. See ADR-0032.
What it does

converts some heat from a hot Reservoir into electricity and rejects the rest into a colder Reservoir. This is the explicit thermal-to-power component, not a negative Equipment load or a discount on radiator heat.
Interfaces

hot Reservoir input, rejection Reservoir output, automatic net generation to the shared electrical pool. Reservoirs must be distinct; the rejection Reservoir must match the engine's thermal class, while the hot Reservoir need not share that class. Outage/Maintenance can target its installation identity through its Supervision port. Place a Heat engine from the Thermal group in Flow's Place node menu (or the canvas context menu). Connect a Reservoir's Heat out to Thermal intake, and Rejection heat to a different Reservoir's Heat in. Power out connects automatically, like other generators. Select the engine to edit its reservoir references, operating settings, mechanical-seizure opt-in, efficiency-drift Wear, and repair-parts plans in the Flow Inspector. Placement starts unwired; Apply uses the normal validated configuration path once both thermal interfaces are connected. Wiring, inspector edits, rename and cascade deletion participate in draft undo/redo.

rows.name: Rated thermal input kW
rows.description: Maximum heat intake, not electrical rating; zero disables.

rows.name: Commanded input kW
rows.description: Intake ceiling within rating; omission in a loaded document means full rated.

rows.name: Carnot fraction
rows.description: Fraction (0,1] of 1 − T_cold/T_hot captured; temperatures in that ratio are kelvin. Actual efficiency changes with the gradient.

rows.name: Auxiliary power kW
rows.description: Parasitic running draw deducted from gross electrical output.

rows.name: Minimum hot temperature °C
rows.description: Source gate below which the engine idles; must be above the maximum sink-temperature gate.

rows.name: Maximum sink temperature °C
rows.description: Rejection gate; at/above it the engine trips until the sink recovers.

rows.name: Thermal class
rows.description: Class of rejection heat, not necessarily that of the hot source.

blocks.text: No gradient, insufficient heat, auxiliaries exceeding gross output, a constrained generation connection or no demand/battery charge headroom can limit/stop conversion. Unconverted heat stays in the hot Reservoir.
Example

recover part of a Generator's hot waste-heat output in a bottoming cycle. Send rejection heat to a dedicated cooler Reservoir and Radiator. Retain a direct hot-side rejection path as needed; when the electrical pool cannot accept power, the engine is not a guaranteed cooling path.
What it does
owns one compartment's volume, gas masses, water vapour and thermal state. Pressure/partial pressures follow the ideal-gas model. Sharing an ID, label or thermal class does not make compartments mix.
Ports

Gas out serves extraction processes/Airlock cycles; Oxygen in accepts direct Electrolyzer supply. Biology in/out bind Crew/Crops/Algae gas, moisture and heat exchanges. Hosted pathways and Thermal links host those two-ended aggregates. Optional Heat out names a Reservoir for a bidirectional heat-only exchanger, not a gas destination.

rows.name: Volume m³
rows.description: Positive contained gas volume; mass and temperature determine pressure.

rows.name: Starting O2 / N2 / CO2 / water vapour kg
rows.description: Independent initial inventories, not composition percentages. Supersaturated vapour condenses with accounted latent heat.

rows.name: Starting temperature °C
rows.description: Initial compartment temperature, above absolute zero.

rows.name: Thermal capacity kJ/K
rows.description: Effective air-plus-structure capacity; controls temperature response.

rows.name: Advected specific heat kJ/kg·K
rows.description: Heat carried per kg of departing pathway gas; positive, separate from thermal capacity.

rows.name: Reservoir / exchanger conductance kW/K
rows.description: Optional heat-only coupling. Without a Reservoir, no exchange occurs through this interface.

rows.name: Occupants
rows.description: Optional simple configured load count; not World Agent count.

rows.name: O2 use / CO2 production / moisture per occupant kg/s
rows.description: Simple occupancy loads, independent of the richer Crew component.

rows.name: Sensible heat per occupant kW
rows.description: Simple occupancy heat. Do not double-count Crew metabolism with these values.

rows.name: Leak rate kg/s
rows.description: Constant composition-proportional external gas loss, capped by inventory. Separate from exterior pathways and Airlock cycles.

rows.name: Minimum/maximum pressure kPa
rows.description: Required positive ordered service limits; report crossings, do not regulate pressure.

rows.name: Minimum O2 / maximum CO2 partial pressure kPa
rows.description: Optional quality limits; zero means unconfigured. Reporting limits do not add oxygen or scrub CO2.

blocks.text: Example

a cabin receives oxygen from an Electrolyzer, loses CO2 through a capture unit and vapour through a Water collector. Crew exchanges gas/heat with it. Couple it to a Reservoir for thermal control and to another Atmosphere through a pathway only if real mixing should occur.
What it does

represents an undirected gas opening. Each tracked gas (O2, N2, CO2, water vapour) moves down its own partial-pressure gradient. Opposing species flows are possible even at equal total pressure. Moving gas also carries sensible heat (Advected enthalpy); this is not pure conduction.
Ports

End A/B join Atmosphere Hosted pathways. Two distinct compartments are valid; alternatively exactly one endpoint can be the reserved $exterior vacuum boundary. Exterior is inert and has no draggable port: set that endpoint through configuration rather than treating it as a tank. Stores and Reservoirs are not valid gas endpoints.

rows.name: Area m²
rows.description: Positive opening area; no separate throughput ceiling.

rows.name: Open percentage / openFraction
rows.description: Effective openness, [0,1] internally; zero shuts exchange.

rows.name: End A / End B
rows.description: Endpoint references and sign convention, not inlet/outlet direction.

blocks.text: Greater area/openness increases exchange at the same state; equalization reduces the driving gradients. Changing openness therefore affects gas-carried heat, but does not modify a separate Thermal link. A closed pathway transfers neither gas nor pathway-carried heat. There is no transport-loss or efficiency setting. Openness can also be actuated by simulation-time-stamped runtime commands; this is not an additional placeable schedule node.
Example

use one pathway for an opening between cabin and greenhouse, and schedule its openness for ventilation. Use another to $exterior for a vent-to-space scenario: lost gas is accounted, and its source can cool as it vents. This is an exchange model, not full pressure-driven fluid dynamics.
What it does

removes a specified mass of gas from a compartment at scheduled times, splitting it into recovered and externally lost gas. This is a Station scenario event, not a movement-system Airlock or its doors.
Ports

Atmosphere joins one compartment's Gas out. No recoverable-gas Store output is currently exposed: recovered mass is retained/accounted in the recovery receiver, not automatically usable breathing supply.

rows.name: Gas mass kg
rows.description: Positive total requested removal per occurrence.

rows.name: Recovered fraction
rows.description: Fraction [0,1] of actual removal recovered; remainder is lost.

rows.name: First occurrence / recurrence
rows.description: Cycle timing, zero recurrence for one-off.

rows.name: Priority
rows.description: Orders coincident events.

blocks.text: Example

model ten daily EVA depressurizations, each removing a declared mass with 80% recovery. Compare lost-gas endurance with an otherwise identical configuration at 95% recovery. Do not also count the same vent as pathway loss.
What it does
splits water into stoichiometric O2 and H2 using electricity. Products retain chemical energy; the remaining electrical dose is process heat.
Ports

Water in uses a plain or compound mass Store, but an immutable zero-dissolved-load runtime gate stops splitting dirty feed. Hydrogen out requires a plain mass Store. Configure exactly one oxygen destination: Oxygen out to a plain mass Store, or Compartment oxygen to an Atmosphere's Oxygen in. Water and gas roles must use distinct Stores. Heat out needs a same-class Reservoir; Power in is automatic.

rows.name: Rate kg/s
rows.description: Rated water split, not oxygen production; zero disables.

rows.name: Specific energy kWh/kg water
rows.description: Electrical dose, at least the chemical energy retained by the products.

rows.name: Thermal class / heat sink
rows.description: Process-heat interface.

rows.name: Maximum sink temperature °C

blocks.text: Example

treat recovered water, feed an Electrolyzer, send oxygen directly to the cabin and hydrogen to Sabatier. To also stockpile oxygen, use a separate Electrolyzer configured for an O2 Store; one unit cannot use both oxygen outlets.
#### Optional casing (thermalBody, #854)
Author an optional shared settings block on the Electrolyzer:
yaml thermalBody: heatCapacityKJPerK: 100 startingTemperatureC: 20 sinkConductanceKWPerK: 0.5

Capacity and sink conductance must be finite and strictly positive; starting temperature must be finite and above absolute zero. Waste heat charges this lumped casing rather than entering the Reservoir directly. Heat out now drains the casing through the shared closed-form two-body conduction law, limited by the wire's throughput and efficiency. Unaccepted heat stays in the casing; wire loss remains an explicitly booked loss. Sink class/qualification still apply to this drain leg. The maximum-temperature gate and coarse-step protection instead read the casing temperature. The casing continues cooling while production is idle or refused, allowing restart after cooling.

A refused sink leg leaves the casing to warm until protection refuses production. With a body, the Heat-out sink is optional: Thermal links may cool the casing into an Atmosphere, Reservoir or another body. Without any heat path, the casing warms to its protection limit and configuration reports a warning. With no thermalBody, the historical direct heat-injection path and serialized representation are unchanged. Bodies are reconstructed from authored starting temperature on load/Reset. The inspector's Thermal body checkbox adds/removes the block in the draft. Capacity, starting temperature and sink conductance support live-node edits; adding/removing a body requires Apply. Live scalar edits preserve the current temperature and physical charge/conduction totals, rebasing the energy reference for the changed capacity or starting value rather than creating a spurious energy residual. Changing the starting value live does not reset the casing temperature.

Published casing fields are hasThermalBody, bodyTemperatureC, lastBodyChargeKW, lastSinkLegKW, bodyChargeKJ, sinkLegKJ, and bodyResidualKJ. Charge plus net conducted heat minus sink outflow equals the casing's capacity times its temperature change (with an energy-reference adjustment after live capacity/starting-value edits). Body temperature and both rates are selectable Electrolyzer observations. Binary World and Station YAML persistence use schema 123 only when a body is present. Station Flow shows a Thermal body face only when that block exists, with live body temperature and signed conducted kW. The link inspector's endpoint picker offers Atmosphere, Reservoir and Thermal body entries; canvas wiring validates endpoints and reports refusals. Body conduction is reported separately from its sink leg.
What it does
extracts CO2 from an Atmosphere into finite storage, spending electricity and any configured regeneration consumable. It does not destroy carbon or implicitly discharge it to space.
Ports

Atmosphere joins Gas out; Captured CO2 out requires a plain mass Store. Optional Consumable in uses a mass Store (plain or compound), and must be wired if a positive consumable rate is declared. Power in is automatic. There is no authored heat-sink port on this component.

blocks.text: Example

a cabin scrubber fills a CO2 Store that feeds Sabatier. If hydrogen runs out, captured-gas storage eventually fills and CO2 capture becomes backpressured even though the scrubber still has nameplate capacity.
What it does
condenses compartment water vapour onto a circulating cold surface, depositing pure condensate into a raw-water Store. The condensation's latent heat goes into the coolant loop exactly once.
Ports

Atmosphere joins Gas out; Cooling loop joins Coolant loop Cold surfaces; Raw water out needs a plain mass Store. The collector's thermal class must match the loop's host Reservoir. The diagram includes an automatic power relationship, but this component has no independent electrical dose/pump-power dial; its real cold surface depends on the loop/thermal plant.

blocks.text: Collection requires actual circulation, a surface colder than the air, vapour above the target and destination headroom. It cannot obtain water from coolant.
Example

collect Crew moisture using a Chiller-cooled loop, store condensate as raw water, then send it through Water treatment. Losing pump power blocks collection even if the raw-water tank is empty and cabin humidity is high.
What it does

processes a water stream into treated output and retained concentrate, consuming electricity and treatment material. Full electrical evidence qualifies the treated product; partial power leaves it held.
Ports

Raw water in, Treated water out, Concentrate out require three distinct mass Stores. Plain or compound streams are supported. Any outlet receiving dry constituents must be compound; full removal permits a plain treated outlet. Consumable in also requires a mass Store. Power in is automatic. The current treatment draws qualified source stock above its reserve, not held stock. Merely feeding a held treated-water Store back into another treatment does not provide a requalification path.

blocks.text: Treatment does not automatically make water acceptable to every consumer: qualified output can still contain dissolved load when removal is partial. Compound concentrate is a qualified product retaining its constituents; legacy plain concentrate is held. Both consume finite storage. There is no separate release-test consumable or hazard-class release switch.
Example

treat 100 kg/day greywater containing 0.2 kg organics with 85% water recovery and full organic removal. Ideal outputs are 84.83 kg/day pure treated water and 15.17 kg/day concentrate. Retain/eject the concentrate; merely adding a treated-water tank does not provide waste capacity.
What it does

consumes food, water and atmospheric oxygen and returns CO2, moisture, heat, urine, organic waste and optionally greywater. Missing input or full return storage scales metabolism and all returns together.
Ports

Food in, Water in, Urine out, Organic waste out require four distinct compound mass Stores. Optional Greywater out also needs a distinct compound mass Store if enabled. Oxygen uptake, CO2 return, Moisture return, Metabolic heat bind the same Atmosphere. No automatic Crew electricity input is declared.

blocks.text: Coefficients must fund all returned mass, constituents and heat from consumed resources. Any unreturned mass is explicitly retained body mass, not silently lost. Configure simple Atmosphere occupancy loads separately or leave them zero to avoid double-counting this Crew.
Example

connect a pantry and potable-water Store to a six-person Crew. Route greywater to treatment and organic waste/urine to recovery installations; CO2 capture and water collection serve its Atmosphere. A full urine tank can limit supplied metabolism even with adequate food and oxygen.
Shared biological requirements

Crew, Crops and Algae use a single Atmosphere reference for their multiple gas/moisture/heat faces. Wiring one face binds the exchange bundle; you cannot send their CO2 to one compartment and their heat to another through those faces. Their populations are authored aggregates, not World Agents. Biological coefficients are tunable assumptions, not validated physiology, agronomy or phycology.

Crew water, crop irrigation, algae makeup and microbial process water support optional water quality tolerances: per-dry-constituent and/or total-dissolved limits in kg constituent/kg stream. Omission means no gate. They read the actual current blend. Above tolerance, operation is scaled to fit the declared full-demand dissolved-load budget; a zero tolerance blocks nonzero load. This is throughput/load limiting, not purification or a health simulation.
What it does

maintains dry living biomass, grows under light and resource supply, respires day and night, transpires water and can harvest food/waste. Living biomass, growing capacity and stored food are different inventories.
Ports

Water in accepts plain/compound mass irrigation. Nitrogen in, Phosphorus in, Potassium in, Minerals in each need their own mass Store; compound fertilizer Stores must be pure in that port's constituent. All five inputs must be distinct. Optional Food out/Waste out become required when harvesting is enabled; mass destinations must be distinct and, if compound, match the declared living composition. The six biological faces (including Photosynthesis CO2/oxygen) bind one Atmosphere. Power in is automatic for circulation and lamps.

blocks.text: Full destinations constrain harvest rather than deleting living mass. Starved organic biomass can be respired away; remaining dead residue goes to waste or is reported as explicit uncontained loss if it cannot be contained.
Example

build a hydroponic greenhouse with compound irrigation, separate fertilizer Stores, artificial lighting and an Atmosphere. Add a purge Transfer and treated makeup supply so salts left by selective uptake do not accumulate until water-quality tolerances throttle growth. Harvest into a compatible food Store, or use a Conversion before mixing a different food composition.

Ports

blocks.text: Example

grow Algae on cabin CO2, send edible harvest to food and recovery harvest to a composition-compatible feed Store for a Microbial processor. Retain inedible residue separately. The processor's nutrients are recovery, not a replacement for the light and water needed to grow new biomass.

What it does
an aerobic waste digester/nutrient-recovery stage with finite feed throughput and aggregate culture condition. It recovers bound nutrients, water and CO2, retains residue and releases funded heat.
Ports

Feed in requires a compound mass Store; Oxygen in a plain mass Store; Water in a plain/compound mass Store. Culture medium must resolve to a Store in a complete configuration (despite its optional Flow appearance); in CompositionDerived mode it must be mass-denominated. Optional Replacement stock may use a Store's native unit. Nutrients out and Residue out require plain mass Stores; CO2 out a plain mass Store; Water out permits compound mass, required for positive dissolved carry-over. All stream roles must use distinct Stores. Heat out joins a same-class Reservoir; Power in is automatic.

blocks.text: Residue is the mass-balance remainder, not an independent yield knob. Outputs cannot exceed funded mass/constituents/energy. Atmospheric nitrogen in feed is not a nutrient resource. Condition coefficients are provisional biological assumptions, not a simulation of individual microbes.
Example

digest Crew organic waste with oxygen, process water, medium and power. Recover mixed nutrients and water, capture CO2 for Sabatier and send residue to Waste ejection storage. Mixed recovered nutrients cannot simply be wired into all four pure fertilizer ports: model the necessary constituent- balanced separation/processing and compatible storage explicitly.

What it does
imports a resource from outside the station at scheduled times. Unlike Transfer, it does not consume another station Store.
Ports
Destination joins one Store's Inventory in; delivery unit must exactly match it. No external source node/port needs to be wired.

blocks.text: Only available capacity is accepted; the rest is explicitly rejected at the external boundary, not silently added later or overflowed.
Example

a cargo flight delivers 200 kg to a food Store every month. With only 50 kg headroom on arrival, only 50 kg is accepted. Schedule pantry Transfers after delivery if they should use the newly arrived inventory.
What it does
removes eligible Store inventory across the external boundary at scheduled times, accounting it as loss. There is no waste recovery output.
Ports
Source joins Store Inventory out; exact native unit match. The eligibility selector, not a hazard or waste label, determines which partition may be removed.

blocks.text: Insufficient eligible material produces a smaller/zero ejection, not a software failure. Removing held contents requires an explicit held-eligible setting.
Example
eject held plain treatment concentrate weekly using HeldOnly; eject qualified compound concentrate using QualifiedOnly. A default qualified selector will not clear a tank whose contents are all held.
What it does
temporarily reduces the rated availability of a registered installation. It is a capacity constraint, not destruction or inventory reset.
Ports
Target installation names a Generator, Coolant loop, Chiller or Heat engine. All four have editable Flow Supervision ports.

rows.name: Capacity fraction
rows.description: Fraction [0,1) of rated capacity remaining, not fraction lost. Zero is a full outage.

rows.description: Window start, positive window length and repetition.

rows.description: Deterministic event announcement/order.

blocks.text: Overlapping reductions take the minimum fraction. Restoration does not refill fuel, coolant, batteries, buffers or biomass.
Example
reduce a Chiller to 50% for ten minutes and watch its Thermal buffer absorb the deficit. Setting the fraction to 0.5 leaves half capacity; it is not a command to halve the sink temperature.
What it does

reserves tools/parts, isolates a registered installation, runs timed work and books consumed supplies into waste on completion. Absent prerequisites delay/block work rather than allowing free maintenance.
Ports

Target installation has the same registered targets as Outage. One to eight Requirement inputs join distinct Stores. Waste out is required if any requirement is consumed; its Store must match consumed input units and compound composition and must not alias those sources. Reusable tools return to their original Stores; no extra return port needs authoring.

rows.name: First occurrence / duration / recurrence
rows.description: Start opportunity and required continuous work time; recurrence cannot overlap its own window.

rows.name: Requirement quantity
rows.description: Positive native units reserved for the job.

rows.name: Requirement consumed
rows.description: False reserves/returns a tool unchanged; true spends it at completion and deposits it as used material/waste.

rows.name: Requirement count
rows.description: One to eight prerequisites.

rows.name: Waste Store
rows.description: Finite headroom for the total consumed requirements.

rows.name: Priority
rows.description: Orders competing reservations.

blocks.text: Active work holds target availability at zero. If reservations/headroom can no longer be maintained, work is interrupted, released and must restart for its full duration. Completion restores availability, not consumables or fuel.
Example

service a coolant pump using reusable tools plus a spare filter. The loop stops while work is active; the filter moves into compatible waste storage at completion and tools return. Provide another cooling path or enough thermal storage to cover the isolation interval.
Purpose/interfaces

derived aggregate connecting all automatic electrical supply/demand/charge/discharge relationships. It owns no authored inventory or manual ports and is not placeable. There is no independent bus-capacity dial.
Controls/example

station dispatch mode is Manual (Generator/Fuel cell commands) or Automatic (commands generators first, then fuel-cell backup to cover demand remaining after solar, subject to real availability). Batteries bridge remaining deficits within their limits. Use Solar + Battery + Equipment to model an eclipse power budget; drawing a bus edge does not grant power.
Purpose/interfaces
derived per-thermal-class service supplied by Chillers and requested by CoolingService Equipment. Not a material Store, a cold Reservoir, or a manually assignable chiller-to-load pipe.
Controls/example
no independent dials; Chiller class/capacity and Equipment class/heat demand determine it. A low laboratory load cannot borrow spare warm service merely because the diagram has both nodes.
Purpose/interfaces

derived vacuum boundary for an Atmosphere pathway with one $exterior endpoint. It has zero species partial pressures and no owned volume, mass or temperature. It is neither editable nor draggable as a peer.
Controls/example

no boundary dials; author pathway area/openness. A vent pathway loses gas to Exterior. A Radiator instead exchanges with its own configured radiative environment; a Thermal link cannot conduct to Exterior.

A prefab packages ordinary components and internal wiring with exposed ports and dials; it does not add a new physical process or bypass any of the rules above. For example, package a Reservoir, Coolant loop and Radiator as a reusable cooling assembly. Check the constituent components when sizing it, and wire only its deliberately exposed interfaces.

blocks.text: Example

retain one hour of one-second observations to compare battery endurance and thermal excursions across eclipse runs. Charts, forecasts, limiters and event logs observe the system; none supplies missing resources.
